prompt: During a partition, what does CAP say each running machine has to choose between?
hint: Think of `n3`, cut off, with a customer waiting.

choices.text: Answering now, or refusing until it is sure its answer is still current
choices.why: Right: answer and risk being stale, or refuse and stay correct.

choices.text: Accepting writes, or accepting reads, but not both kinds of request
choices.why: A node that chose consistency refused both the write and the read in the capture.

choices.text: Answering quickly, or answering correctly, on every ordinary request
choices.why: That is the trade-off PACELC names for the days with no partition.

choices.text: Tolerating the partition, or shutting down until it ends
choices.why: P is not a choice: the cut happens either way, and the question is what to do during it.

prompt: Why is "pick any two of C, A and P" the wrong picture for a system on several machines?
hint: Who decides whether a partition happens?

choices.text: With enough replicas, a system can in fact have all three at once
choices.why: More replicas do not stop a cut; they only change how many nodes sit on each side.

choices.text: The network decides whether it happens, so P is not a choice
choices.why: Right: the only choice left is C or A while the cut lasts.

choices.text: C and A turn out to be one property under two names
choices.why: They are opposite answers to the same cut: refuse, or answer.

choices.text: Partitions no longer happen inside one modern data centre
choices.why: They are rarer, but a cable, a switch or a slow peer still produces one.

prompt: What does the C of CAP mean?
hint: It is not the C of ACID.

choices.text: A transaction leaves the database’s rules intact
choices.why: That is the C of ACID, a different word with the same letter.

choices.text: Every copy of a table has the same set of columns
choices.why: That is about the schema; CAP is about which value a read returns.

choices.text: Every read sees the latest completed write, as if there were one copy
choices.why: Right: linearisability, as though there were one copy.

choices.text: Data passes its quality checks before it is stored
choices.why: Checks at the door are lesson 7; they say nothing about copies agreeing.

prompt: Which of these are true of availability as CAP defines it? Choose all that apply.
hint: The definition is about each machine, not the month.

choices.text: Every running machine that gets a request answers it
choices.why: Yes: that is the definition in the proof.

choices.text: An error does not count as an answer
choices.why: Yes: refusing with an error is exactly what giving up availability looks like.

choices.text: It is measured as the share of the month the service was up
choices.why: That is uptime, a measurement over time and another sense of the word.

choices.text: The majority side answering is enough to count as available
choices.why: Then the system chose consistency: the minority side refused.

prompt: The consistency of CAP has a precise name: ___.
hint: As though there were one copy, read in a line.

prompt: In the `cp` run, on how many nodes was `n1`’s write of 5 recorded?
hint: Read the line that starts `n1 write 5`.

prompt: In the `cp` run, why did `n3` refuse the read as well as the write?
hint: What could `n3` not know about its own copy?

choices.text: The partition had wiped its copy of the count
choices.why: Its copy still said 6; the cut removes nothing.

choices.text: It could not know whether the majority had accepted a write it never saw
choices.why: Right: the majority might have accepted a write it never saw, and it had.

choices.text: Once a node refuses one write, it refuses everything after it
choices.why: Both refusals come from the same check, the majority, made afresh each time.

choices.text: It had seen the newer value on `n2` and would not contradict it
choices.why: It could not see `n2` at all: that is what the cut means.

prompt: In the `ap` run, what did a read from `n3` return?
hint: The line `n3 read:`.

prompt: In the `ap` run, `n2` read 5 and `n3` read 7. Which statement is true?
hint: One bicycle left, one came back.

choices.text: `n3` is right, because its write came later than `n1`’s
choices.why: Later is not truer: `n3` never saw the ride taken at `n1`.

choices.text: `n2` is right, because it sits on the majority side
choices.why: In `ap` mode the majority decides nothing, and `n2` never saw the return.

choices.text: Neither one is the true count of bicycles there
choices.why: Right: Rua XV holds 6, and each node saw half of what happened.

choices.text: Both are right until somebody compares them
choices.why: Each is a faithful report of what one node saw, and neither is the count.

prompt: A store that chose consistency runs on two nodes, and the link between them is cut. What happens to writes?
hint: Is one of two more than half?

choices.text: The node that was leader keeps accepting them
choices.why: The leader also sees one of two, which is not a majority.

choices.text: Both sides accept them and merge after the cut
choices.why: That is the AP behaviour, which this store did not choose.

choices.text: The node holding the newer data keeps accepting them
choices.why: Neither node can tell whether the other is newer without talking to it.

choices.text: Both sides refuse, because neither holds a majority
choices.why: Right: that is why such systems run three or five nodes.

prompt: Why can a real node not know it is partitioned, as `replicas.py` lets it?
hint: Lesson 9: what can a timeout tell apart?

choices.text: Networks report a cut to the routers and not to the nodes themselves
choices.why: Nothing reports a cut to anybody; the symptom is silence.

choices.text: Silence from a cut peer looks like a slow one
choices.why: Right: a timeout cannot tell a cut, a slow peer and a dead one apart.

choices.text: Nodes keep no clock with which to measure a wait
choices.why: They have clocks; the trouble is that waiting does not explain itself.

choices.text: Detecting a partition needs a vote of every node first
choices.why: A vote would need the very messages the cut is losing.

prompt: What lets a CP system be sure only one side of a cut accepts writes?
hint: Two groups cannot both have it.

choices.text: The side with the newest clock reading wins
choices.why: Clocks disagree, and a cut gives no way to compare them.

choices.text: Only one side of any cut ever holds a majority of the nodes
choices.why: Right: two of three on one side leaves no second majority anywhere.

choices.text: The client picks the side at random for each request
choices.why: A random pick could land on both sides over two requests.

choices.text: Every write is copied to a backup before it is accepted
choices.why: A backup is a copy, not a rule about who may write.

prompt: Match each cost of choosing consistency to when it is paid.
hint: Only one of them waits for a partition.

pairs.right: only while a link is cut

pairs.left: each write waits for a majority
pairs.right: on every write, cut or not

pairs.left: writes stop until a new leader is chosen

prompt: Which Roda Livre action belongs on the side that refuses during a cut?
hint: Could two yeses be undone?

choices.text: Showing the dock map to a customer about to walk
choices.why: A map slightly behind still helps; an error does not.

choices.text: Unlocking `B017` for a customer
choices.why: Right: one bicycle cannot be handed to two riders.

choices.text: Recording a reading sent by a dock sensor
choices.why: A reading is a fact that merges; a duplicate is dropped by its id.

choices.text: Counting yesterday’s rides for the morning report
choices.why: That reads a copy kept behind on purpose; no cut is involved.

prompt: A payment refused during a cut, or a payment accepted on both sides. Why is the refusal the better failure?
hint: Lesson 1 named two kinds of failure.

choices.text: A refusal is loud, and the client is free to try it again safely
choices.why: Right, and an idempotent retry makes it safe; a double charge succeeds twice in silence.

choices.text: A double charge is merged into one at the end of the day
choices.why: A charge is a decision, not a count: there is nothing to merge it with.

choices.text: Customers prefer an error message to a short delay
choices.why: The argument is about which failure can be undone, not about taste.

choices.text: On a CP system a payment cannot be charged twice in any case
choices.why: A careless client can still send it twice; the refusal is what stops the cut doing so.

prompt: Which cost of choosing consistency is paid on a day when nothing is broken?
hint: The theorem does not mention it.

choices.text: The minority side of the network refuses requests
choices.why: That needs a cut; on a calm day there is no minority side.

choices.text: Copies diverge and have to be merged later
choices.why: That is the bill of the AP side.

choices.text: Each write waits until a majority has answered
choices.why: Right: PACELC calls this the latency side of the trade.

choices.text: Every read compares timestamps across all the copies
choices.why: Comparing timestamps is last write wins, an AP technique.

prompt: In `merge.py`, why did last write wins keep 7?
hint: Look at the two `at` fields.

choices.text: The rule always keeps whichever value is larger
choices.why: It compares times, not values; a later 5 would have won.

choices.text: The return was stamped 08:05, which is later than the ride’s 08:02
choices.why: Right: 08:05 beats 08:02, and the ride is thrown away.

choices.text: The node that was cut off has the final say once it is back
choices.why: Which node was cut does not enter the rule at all.

choices.text: A return cancels any ride taken from the same station
choices.why: The rule knows nothing of rides or returns, only timestamps.

prompt: What count did the merged counter in `merge.py` give for ST02?
hint: The line `merged counter:`.

prompt: What makes the counter safe to merge whenever two copies meet? Choose all that apply.
hint: The last two lines of the output test two of them.

choices.text: The order of a merge makes no difference
choices.why: Yes: "either order: True".

choices.text: Merging the same copy twice changes nothing
choices.why: Yes: "merged twice: True".

choices.text: Each node counts only what it saw itself
choices.why: Yes: that is what lets the merge take the larger number per node.

choices.text: The merge keeps the copy with the latest timestamp
choices.why: That is last write wins, the rule that lost a bicycle.

choices.text: The nodes elect a leader before they merge anything
choices.why: No leader is needed; that is the point of the shape.

prompt: A data type built so that any two of its copies can be merged is called a ___.
hint: Four capital letters, named in 2011.

prompt: Why does last write wins depend on the nodes’ clocks?
hint: Lesson 9: clocks disagree.

choices.text: Clocks decide which node becomes leader after a cut
choices.why: Last write wins has no leader; it only compares stamps.

choices.text: A fast clock lets an earlier write win
choices.why: Right: the stamp, not the moment, decides.

choices.text: Two writes with the same stamp are both thrown away
choices.why: A tie needs some rule, but the danger is a stamp that is wrong.

choices.text: The merge counts the seconds between the two writes
choices.why: It compares two stamps and keeps one; it counts nothing.

prompt: Why did Dynamo’s shopping cart suit the side that answers during a cut?
hint: What happens to two versions of one cart?

choices.text: Carts are too small for a partition to affect them
choices.why: Size has nothing to do with it; any copied value can diverge.

choices.text: Carts are stored on one machine, out of reach of the network
choices.why: They were replicated, which is why two versions could exist.

choices.text: Two carts merge cleanly, and an error loses the sale
choices.why: Right: a wrong cart for a minute is cheaper than a refused click.

choices.text: Customers expect their cart to be out of date
choices.why: Nobody expects it; the merge makes it rarely visible.

prompt: What does the E in PACELC stand for?
hint: Read the name as a sentence.

choices.text: Eventual, as in eventual consistency
choices.why: A tempting reading, but the letters spell an if and an else.

choices.text: Error, the reply a refusing node sends
choices.why: Refusing belongs to the P half; E opens the other half.

choices.text: Election, of a new leader after a crash
choices.why: Elections exist, but they are not in the name.

choices.text: Else: what to choose when nothing is partitioned
choices.why: Right: else, choose latency or consistency.

prompt: Why is there a choice between latency and consistency when nothing is broken?
hint: What does being sure wait for?

choices.text: A consistent read has to scan every row of the data set
choices.why: Consistency is about which copy answers, not how much is read.

choices.text: Detecting partitions slows every request down a little
choices.why: The wait is for agreement, and it is there with or without detection.

choices.text: Agreeing with another copy costs a message there and back
choices.why: Right: waiting for another copy is what being sure costs.

choices.text: Consistent systems write every record to disk twice
choices.why: Disk writes are not what the letters describe.

prompt: Match each PACELC pair to what the system does.
hint: The first letter pair is the cut; the second is the calm day.

pairs.right: answers during a cut, answers fast otherwise
refuses during a cut, waits for agreement otherwise
answers during a cut, waits for agreement otherwise
refuses during a cut, answers fast otherwise

prompt: Cassandra keeps three copies. Which levels make a read see the last write?
hint: Lesson 9: R + W > N.

choices.text: `ONE` for writes and `QUORUM` for reads
choices.why: 1 + 2 = 3, which is not more than 3: the read can miss the copy that took the write.

choices.text: `QUORUM` for both
choices.why: Right: 2 + 2 = 4 > 3, so the two always share a copy.

choices.text: `ONE` for both, on a fast enough network
choices.why: Speed does not help: 1 + 1 can name two different copies.

choices.text: `QUORUM` for writes and `ONE` for reads
choices.why: 2 + 1 = 3 again: the one copy read may be the one the write skipped.

prompt: Match each consistency model to the surprise it rules out at Roda Livre.
hint: Two of them are promises to one session.

pairs.right: a reader seeing 7 after another was told 5
ana’s finished ride still showing as open
the map going from 6 back to 5
copies that never agree once writes stop

prompt: ana returns a bicycle and the app still shows her ride as open. Which guarantee is missing?
hint: It is about her own action.

choices.text: Monotonic reads
choices.why: That stops going backwards after seeing something newer; she never saw the return.

choices.text: Read-your-writes
choices.why: Right: her own write should be visible to her.

choices.text: Eventual consistency
choices.why: This is still eventual: the copies will agree later.

choices.text: Partition tolerance
choices.why: Nothing here needs a cut; one lagging copy is enough.

prompt: What does eventual consistency promise?
hint: It says nothing about the meantime.

choices.text: Every read is at most a second behind the latest write
choices.why: It puts no bound on time at all.

choices.text: Copies agree a moment after each write
choices.why: That is how it is heard; it promises less.

choices.text: Copies converge once the writes stop coming
choices.why: Right, and not when, nor what is read on the way.

choices.text: A reader never sees an older value after a newer one
choices.why: That is monotonic reads, a stronger promise.

prompt: Why do read-your-writes and monotonic reads cost less than strong consistency?
hint: Who has to wait?

choices.text: They are promises to one session
choices.why: Right: only that session’s reads are steered or held, nobody else’s.

choices.text: They skip the copies on the far side of the network
choices.why: They may read any copy; what they constrain is which, for one reader.

choices.text: They are only offered on a single machine with no replicas
choices.why: On one machine there would be nothing to promise.

choices.text: They let the copies stop replicating for a while
choices.why: Replication goes on; the promise is about what one reader sees.

prompt: Where does a PostgreSQL database on one machine sit in the figure, and why?
hint: What would a cut separate?

choices.text: On the CP edge, as a consensus system with a leader
choices.why: One machine runs no consensus; there is nobody to agree with.

choices.text: On the AP edge, because a single machine answers everyone
choices.why: Answering everyone is easy when no copy can disagree.

choices.text: Outside the triangle: CAP does not apply to SQL
choices.why: The query language is irrelevant; the number of copies decides.

choices.text: On the C–A edge, because there is no network to cut between copies
choices.why: Right: a second copy would move it to one of the other edges.

prompt: Unclean leader election is off and every in-sync copy of a Kafka partition is gone. What does Kafka do?
hint: Waiting is the C.

choices.text: Promotes the most recent copy that is out of sync
choices.why: That is what switching unclean election on allows, at the price of lost messages.

choices.text: Waits for an in-sync copy to return
choices.why: Right: it refuses rather than lose messages.

choices.text: Accepts writes on every broker and merges them later
choices.why: Kafka keeps one leader per partition and does not merge.

choices.text: Deletes the partition and creates it again, empty
choices.why: Nothing is deleted; the partition is unavailable until a copy returns.

prompt: What changed about Amazon S3 in December 2020?
hint: Workarounds became dead weight.

choices.text: Uploads became eventually consistent to make them faster
choices.why: The change went the other way.

choices.text: It began refusing writes whenever a region was cut off
choices.why: The change was about what a read returns after a write.

choices.text: Overwrites began to be settled by last write wins across regions
choices.why: The section names no such change.

choices.text: Reads straight after a write became strongly consistent
choices.why: Right: an overwritten file is read back in its new version.

prompt: Why is "Cassandra is AP" a statement about a default rather than a fact?
hint: Its consistency level travels with each request.

choices.text: `QUORUM` makes the minority side refuse
choices.why: Right: per request, it can behave as CP.

choices.text: It was mislabelled for years and has really been CP all along
choices.why: By default it answers on both sides; the label is right about the default.

choices.text: It keeps a single copy, so CAP does not apply to it
choices.why: It keeps several copies, which is why the levels exist.

choices.text: In a cluster of three nodes, AP and CP behave the same way
choices.why: The capture showed three nodes behaving in two different ways.

prompt: Which question decides whether a piece of Roda Livre’s data goes on the side that refuses or the side that answers?
hint: Imagine both sides of a cut saying yes.

choices.text: How large the data is, and how quickly it grows each month
choices.why: Volume is lesson 7’s question; it does not decide what a cut should do.

choices.text: Which database the company already runs for its other data
choices.why: That is choosing by letters for the whole company, the mistake the section names.

choices.text: If both sides said yes, could the two answers be merged afterwards?
choices.why: Right: if they merge, answer; if not, refuse.

choices.text: How many people read it on an ordinary day
choices.why: Popular data can sit on either side.

prompt: Which of these can safely answer on both sides of a cut? Choose all that apply.
hint: Ask whether two answers merge.

choices.text: The dock map in the app
choices.why: Yes: counts merge, and a map slightly behind still helps.

choices.text: Readings from the dock sensors
choices.why: Yes: a reading is a fact, and duplicates are dropped by id.

choices.text: The payment for a ride
choices.why: No: a double charge becomes a refund and a phone call.

choices.text: Which customer holds bicycle `B017`
choices.why: No: one bicycle, one rider.

prompt: What does a data platform promise in place of linearisability?
hint: Lesson 2 made it a target.

choices.text: That every copy agrees with the source at every moment
choices.why: That is linearisability itself, which the platform gave up on purpose.

choices.text: Freshness: a known delay, stated in advance and measured
choices.why: Right: behind by an amount it states and measures.

choices.text: That it answers on both sides of any network cut
choices.why: The platform reads a copy; cuts in the app’s store are not its question.

choices.text: That every report is recomputed from the source on each read
choices.why: That would put the platform back on the source’s clock and load.

prompt: Roda Livre adds reservations: a customer can hold a bicycle for ten minutes before riding. Which side should a reservation go on?
hint: Two customers, one bicycle.

choices.text: The answering side, since a reservation is just another entry on the map
choices.why: A map entry merges; two holds on one bicycle do not.

choices.text: Neither: it belongs in the nightly batch with the morning report
choices.why: A reservation is needed now, not tomorrow morning.

choices.text: The refusing side: two holds cannot merge
choices.why: Right: it is the unlock decision, ten minutes early.

choices.text: The answering side, provided timestamps settle any tie afterwards
choices.why: Last write wins would silently cancel one customer’s hold.

prompt: Put the stages of lesson 3’s lifecycle in order.
hint: The middle row of the map, left to right.
trap: Data is stored raw before it is transformed, so the raw copy survives a bad transformation.

prompt: Lesson 7 only introduced checks at the door. Which course takes data quality further?
hint: The transformation stage names two.

choices.text: `statistics`, the next course in the track
choices.why: It teaches what to do with a number once it can be trusted.

choices.text: `data-cleaning`, which measures and repairs it
choices.why: Right: quality measured and repaired in depth.

choices.text: `warehouse-modeling`, which organises the stored data
choices.why: It models the warehouse; quality in depth is another course.

choices.text: `streaming`, which handles late and duplicate events
choices.why: It walks lesson 8’s region, not quality in general.

prompt: Last write wins lost a bicycle and printed nothing. Which of the four recurring ideas is that?
hint: Lesson 1’s `twice.py` was another one.

choices.text: A loud failure, which names itself
choices.why: Nothing stopped and nothing was named: that is the other kind.

choices.text: A copy that somebody declared to be behind
choices.why: A declared delay is honest; this loss was invisible.

choices.text: A quiet failure
choices.why: Right: a plausible wrong number, the kind the profession exists to prevent.

choices.text: A trade-off with a right side in general
choices.why: The section says no trade-off has a right side in general.

prompt: Put the events of the `ap` run, and what follows it, in order.
hint: The cut comes before anything diverges.
items: the link heals and the copies are merged
trap: Divergence needs the cut first, and the merge needs the link back.

prompt: A store that chose consistency has five nodes, and a cut splits them three and two. Which side accepts writes?
hint: More than half of five.

choices.text: The side of two, if the leader happens to be on it
choices.why: Two of five is not a majority; the leader steps down without one.

choices.text: Both sides, until the cut has been detected
choices.why: A CP store checks for a majority before accepting, detected or not.

choices.text: Neither, since no side holds all five nodes
choices.why: A majority is enough; unanimity would make every cut fatal.

choices.text: The side of three, because three of five is a majority
choices.why: Right: three of five is a majority, and there cannot be two.

prompt: During a cut, the app still shows the dock map but greys out the unlock button. What has Roda Livre done?
hint: Two pieces of data, two answers.

choices.text: Chosen availability for the whole app, and failed to deliver it
choices.why: The greyed button is a deliberate refusal, not a failure of AP.

choices.text: Chosen per piece of data: AP map, CP unlock
choices.why: Right: each part of the app got the answer its data needs.

choices.text: Chosen consistency for the whole app, apart from the cache
choices.why: The map answering during a cut is availability, whatever stores it.

choices.text: Avoided the partition by keeping a copy on the phone
choices.why: A copy on the phone is one more copy that can fall behind.

prompt: PACELC: if there is a Partition, choose Availability or Consistency; Else, choose ___ or Consistency.
hint: What you pay to wait for another copy.
